transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I’m here because... honestly, for months now I’ve been trying to get people to understand that my husband’s family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. It’s just so exhausting. Like, little billing errors will just randomly show up at work—I’m a billing clerk, you know. And I’ve always been so careful with numbers. My math teacher in high school, Mr. Henderson, always said I had a real knack for it. He retired a few years ago and moved to Florida... I think it was Boca? Or maybe Sarasota. My aunt lives in Sarasota and she says
Have you ever heard voices, or seen things, that other people around you didn't seem to hear or see?

Voices? No, of course not. I don't hear things like that. My hearing is perfectly fine, though. Actually, it's almost too sharp sometimes. Like, I can hear the hum of our refrigerator all the way from the living room. We just got a new one a couple of years ago because the ice maker broke on the old one. We went with stainless steel this time. I originally wanted the plain white one, because honestly, stainless shows absolutely every single fingerprint. And with my husband's brother always coming over uninvited and digging around for a soda, I am constantly having to wipe the handles down. I use that special spray—you know, the one in the purple can? It smells a little like lavender, which I usually love, but my neighbor grows real lavender in her front yard and the bees are just terrible in the summer. I can't even leave my windows open without them getting in through the screens.
Aside from your concerns about your husband's family, how have you been managing with your job and daily responsibilities lately?

Oh, I'm managing fine, really. I still get up every morning for work, handle all my billing clerk duties, and keep the house going. I even make sure to spend time on my hobbies, like gardening and painting. Actually, I was just out in the garden this past weekend trying to save my hydrangeas. The soil around our foundation is just so acidic, you know? You have to add garden lime if you want the blooms to stay pink, otherwise they turn this deep blue. My grandmother had the most beautiful blue hydrangeas back in Ohio. She used to paint them, too, which is probably where I get my love for watercolors. I buy my brushes from that little craft store on Main Street—the one right next to the bakery that makes those awfully dry scones. I don't know how they stay in business with pastries like that, honestly. My husband bought a blueberry muffin there once and it was practically dust. 

But anyway, yes, my daily routine is perfectly normal. The main trouble only really comes up when I try to warn people about what my in-laws are doing. That's the only thing that gets exhausting, just trying to get anyone to pay attention to it.
Can you tell me approximately how long you've believed that your husband's family has been tampering with your finances and reputation—has it been weeks, months, or longer?

Well, let me think... it’s been about nine months now. Yes, nine months, because it all really started right around the holidays when there was all that trouble with his family over money and holiday expectations. You know how ridiculous people get about the holidays anyway. My sister-in-law just expected everyone to cater to her schedule, and she always brings her little dog over—a Pomeranian, I think? Or maybe a Papillon. It has those big fluffy ears and she just lets it run right into the kitchen while I’m trying to baste the turkey. 

I actually bought a really nice glass baster from one of those kitchen supply catalogs, the ones that send you mail every single week even if you haven't ordered anything in years. It's such a waste of glossy paper, honestly. It fills up my recycling bin so fast, and our recycling truck comes at five in the morning on Thursdays. The driver is so incredibly loud, he just tosses the plastic bins right onto the driveway when he's done. I actually had to go down to the hardware store and buy a new lid for ours because it cracked right down the middle from him throwing it. They didn't even have the dark green lids to match, so now I have a green bin with a bright blue lid, which just looks terrible from the street.
Over these past nine months, have you noticed any changes in your mood, like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually energetic or elated, that lasted for a while?

Sad? Hopeless? No, no, I haven't felt anything like that. I mean, I get frustrated, obviously, because of what they're doing, but my mood is fine. I certainly haven't been running around with crazy energy either. I just keep up my normal pace. 

Speaking of keeping pace, I actually started walking in the mornings before work. Just around the neighborhood, you know? It's supposed to be good for your heart, and honestly, it gets me out of the house before the neighbor's kids start waiting for the school bus. They stand right at the corner of our property and leave candy wrappers in my flower beds. I found a bright pink bubblegum wrapper just yesterday, tucked right under my daylilies. Those daylilies are the Stella d'Oro kind—they bloom almost all summer if you deadhead them properly. I learned how to do that from a gardening show on public television. They play it on Saturday afternoons right after this cooking show where the host always uses way too much butter. I mean, everything looks delicious, but you can't eat like that every day, can you? My husband tried to make one of her recipes once—a chicken piccata, I think—and he used every single pan we own. I was washing dishes for an hour. I buy that dish soap with the little duck on the front, because they say it's gentle on your hands, but my skin still gets so dry in the winter anyway. I have to use this heavy lotion I get from the pharmacy, the one in the pump bottle that always gets clogged when it's about halfway empty.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that husband's family is tampering with finances and reputation) persisting for approximately 9 months. She denies hallucinations, denies mood episode symptoms (depressive or manic), and maintains largely intact occupational, social, and daily functioning aside from preoccupation with the delusional content. Speech is notably circumstantial/tangential but there is no evidence of disorganized thought process impairing communication of core content, no negative symptoms, and no other psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, bizarre delusions, disorganized behavior) required to meet criteria for schizophrenia. This pattern—circumscribed delusion(s) without other active-phase psychotic symptoms, preserved functioning, and duration >1 month—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22), persecutory type.
